pr.title: Extending `#[rustc_force_inline]` to be applicable to inherent methods
pr.description:
`#[rustc_force_inline]` is an internal-only attribute similar to `#[inline(always)]` but which emits an error if inlining cannot occur. rustc_force_inline uses the MIR inliner to do this and has limitations on where it can be applied to ensure that an error is always emitted if inlining can't happen (e.g. it can't be applied to trait methods because calls to those can't always be resolved).

`#[rustc_force_inline]` is motivated by AArch64 pointer authentication intrinsics where it is vital for the security properties of these intrinsics that they do not exist in standalone functions that could be used as gadgets in an exploit (if they could, then you could sign whatever pointers you want, for example, which is bad, but if you force inlining, then you can't jump to a reusable function containing only these instructions).

Since its initial implementation, `#[rustc_force_inline]` could only be applied to free functions. This can be relaxed to also allow inherent methods while still preserving the desired properties. In a work-in-progress patch for manual pointer authentication intrinsics, it is useful to introduce types with inherent methods that would need to be force inlined.

processing.reason: The PR's only compiler change is an attribute-target allowlist update: `RustcForceInlineParser::ALLOWED_TARGETS` gains `Allow(Target::Method(MethodKind::Inherent))`. No MIR value-assignment rewrite is introduced or fixed: the decoded before/after ForceInline dumps show the corrected pipeline replacing `_1 = Foo::bar()` with an `(inlined Foo::bar)` scope, but the historical behavior was simply that the attribute was rejected on inherent methods (diagnostic "`#[rustc_force_inline]` attribute cannot be used on inherent methods") or the call remained an ordinary non-inlined call. That is a compile-time acceptance/feature-enablement difference, not a semantic transformation of runtime values. A self-contained original/transformed function pair would therefore either both compute identical results (non-inlined call vs. inlined call) or require the "original" to fail compilation, so it cannot satisfy the requirement that both variants pass Miri on identical inputs while producing different deterministic values. Any value-altering pair would be an unrelated manufactured rewrite, which the instructions prohibit.

analysis.summary: This PR extends `#[rustc_force_inline]` from free functions to inherent methods. The only compiler change is an attribute-parser allowlist update (`Allow(Target::Method(MethodKind::Inherent))`); the ForceInline pass then inlines calls to such inherent methods and still reports an error if forced inlining is incompatible (e.g. `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]`).
analysis.originalLogic: `RustcForceInlineParser` previously accepted the attribute only on free functions: `const ALLOWED_TARGETS: AllowedTargets = AllowedTargets::AllowList(&[Allow(Target::Fn)]);`. Applying `#[rustc_force_inline]` to an inherent method therefore produced the target diagnostic "`#[rustc_force_inline]` attribute cannot be used on inherent methods", so the method was not a candidate for the ForceInline pass.
analysis.incorrectTransformation: Historically, the compiler refused to accept `#[rustc_force_inline]` on an inherent method and left the call as an ordinary non-inlined `Foo::bar()` / `Foo::callee_forced()` call (or rejected the program outright), instead of treating the inherent method as force-inlined. The corrected behavior allows `Target::Method(MethodKind::Inherent)` and emits MIR where the call is replaced by `scope 1 (inlined Foo::bar)` / `scope 1 (inlined Foo::callee_forced)`. This is a feature-enablement change, not a reproduced miscompile; the historical behavior was an over-restrictive target check, not a wrong algebraic rewrite.
analysis.inputDomain: Rust source using `#![feature(rustc_attrs)]` and `-Copt-level=0 --crate-type=lib`, containing an inherent `impl Foo { ... }` method annotated with `#[rustc_force_inline]`, called as `Foo::method()` from a free function, a closure body, or an async function body. Variants include an inherent method plus a same-named trait method, `-Clink-dead-code`, both panic strategies, and an inherent method also marked `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]` (must fail).
analysis.trigger: A call resolves to an inherent method carrying `#[rustc_force_inline]`; the parser must accept `Target::Method(MethodKind::Inherent)`, after which the ForceInline MIR pass replaces the call with an inlined scope.
preconditions: The attribute is applied to an inherent method inside an `impl` block, not to a trait method, provided trait method, foreign function, closure, expression, statement, or match arm.

The inherent method must not also carry `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]`; if it does, compilation must fail with "`Foo::bar` is incompatible with `#[rustc_force_inline]`" and note "incompatible due to: #[rustc_no_mir_inline]".
MIR-opt tests use `-Copt-level=0 --crate-type=lib` with `// EMIT_MIR_FOR_EACH_PANIC_STRATEGY` and `#![feature(rustc_attrs)]`.
The call target must be resolvable to the inherent method; when a same-named trait method also exists, Rust name resolution still selects the inherent method.
pitfalls: Allowing inherent methods must not relax the force-inline guarantee: the method still must be fully inlined, because `#[rustc_force_inline]` is intended to ensure security-sensitive intrinsics (e.g. AArch64 pointer authentication) do not remain as standalone callable functions.
An inherent method that cannot be inlined (for example due to `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]`) must produce a hard error rather than silently falling back to a normal call.

In an `async` caller, the `ForceInline` MIR dump for the outer async function only creates the coroutine; the call is inside the coroutine body, so the outer dump legitimately shows no `(inlined ...)` scope. Do not infer failure from that dump.
A call inside a closure body is inlined in the closure's MIR (`caller::{closure#0}`), so the expected `(inlined ...)` label appears on the closure function.
Trait methods and provided trait methods remain unsupported targets; only inherent methods are newly allowed.
Inherent-method support is orthogonal to trait-impl ambiguity: the test with both an inherent `Foo::bar` and an `impl Tr for Foo` method confirms the inherent method is selected and force-inlined.
analysis.testStrategy: Add MIR-opt tests that compare before/after `ForceInline` dumps for inherent-method calls, checking for `scope 1 (inlined Foo::bar)` and absence of the standalone call. Cover free-function caller, closure caller (`caller::{closure#0}`), async caller (call occurs in coroutine body), `-Clink-dead-code`, and an inherent method shadowing a trait method, under both `panic-abort` and `panic-unwind`. Add a UI `check-fail` test with both `#[rustc_force_inline]` and `#[rustc_no_mir_inline]` verifying the incompatibility error. Update the invalid-target UI test to remove the expected error for an inherent method while keeping trait methods, foreign functions, closures, expressions, statements, and match arms rejected.
evidence: #[rustc_force_inline]` is an internal-only attribute similar to `#[inline(always)]` but which emits an error if inlining cannot occur.
Since its initial implementation, `#[rustc_force_inline]` could only be applied to free functions. This can be relaxed to also allow inherent methods while still preserving the desired properties.
